metadata.title: Adolescents’ meaning in life as a resilience factor between bullying victimization and life satisfaction

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 nationally representative data for U.S. 15-year-olds and applies the final student weight to produce nationally representative estimates. Sampling followed a two-stage stratified design: 164 schools were sampled within eight strata (four regions × two school types) using PPS, and then 4,838 students were sampled within schools. The analysis also uses Mplus TYPE = COMPLEX RANDOM with stratification and schools treated as a clustering variable to obtain standard errors robust to the non-independence induced by the clustered sampling. The manuscript does not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., TOTWGT), but it explicitly states that the final student weight for national representativeness was applied.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variables are bullying victimization (constructed from questionnaire items), meaning in life (MIL) (questionnaire items), and life satisfaction (a single-item self-report), rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. Missing data handling is described as full information maximum likelihood (FIML) in Mplus, which is treated here as multiple imputation–type handling per the provided mapping. This approach estimates model parameters using all available data under a missing-at-random assumption, rather than deleting cases.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample consists of U.S. adolescents aged 15 years from PISA 2018. The study uses the full nationally representative U.S. student sample drawn through the PISA two-stage stratified design (schools sampled within eight strata; students sampled within schools). No additional grade-subsetting is described beyond the PISA 15-year-old target population. Missingness is handled using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) in Mplus; the manuscript reports missing-value proportions of <6.5% for each indicator and 7.5% for pairwise combinations of indicators.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 U.S. 15-year-olds (bullying victimization, meaning in life, life satisfaction)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Latent moderated structural equations (LMS) in Mplus: Model 0 fit CFI=0.982, TLI=0.968, RMSEA=0.043, SRMR=0.021; Model 1 vs Model 0 log-likelihood ratio test TRd=19.97 (Δdf=1, p<.001). Interaction: B=0.231, SE=0.054, p<.001, β=0.074. Main effects: bullying victimization → life satisfaction B=-0.369, SE=0.038, p<.001, β=-0.168; MIL → life satisfaction B=1.861, SE=0.060, p<.001, β=0.511.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 U.S. 15-year-olds the study leveraged bullying victimization, meaning in life (MIL), and their interaction (controlling for gender and ESCS) to predict life satisfaction, finding that bullying victimization was negatively related to life satisfaction while MIL was positively related, and that the bullying victimization × MIL interaction was significant and positive (i.e., MIL buffered the negative association). This indicates that strengthening adolescents’ meaning in life may mitigate the harm of bullying victimization on well-being, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 nationally representative data for U.S. 15-year-olds to test whether meaning in life (MIL) functions as both a compensatory and protective resilience factor between bullying victimization and life satisfaction. Bullying victimization is measured with six frequency items (verbal, physical, relational), MIL with three comprehension/purpose/meaning items, and life satisfaction with a single 0–10 item. Using Mplus latent moderated structural equations (LMS) with TYPE = COMPLEX RANDOM and the final student weight, the authors report good measurement-model fit (CFI=0.982, TLI=0.968, RMSEA=0.043, SRMR=0.021) and a significant improvement from Model 0 to Model 1 (TRd=19.97, p<.001). The key moderation effect is significant (interaction B=0.231, SE=0.054, p<.001), with bullying victimization negatively related to life satisfaction (B=-0.369) and MIL positively related (B=1.861). Limitations include cross-sectional data (no causal inference) and the use of non-PV self-report outcomes rather than achievement PVs.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This paper is not an empirical machine-learning prediction study: it uses latent moderated structural equations (LMS) with confirmatory factor analysis and FIML for missing data, rather than training ML algorithms. Therefore, ml_techniques are intentionally left empty and no ML performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE from predictive models) are applicable. The extracted findings are substantive statistical relationships and moderation effects estimated within a structural equation modeling framework.
